Series::log2¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::log2() const -> Series
Series& Series::log2_()
Series& Series::log2_() const

What It Does¶

log2() is the base-2 logarithm, applied elementwise: log2(x) is the power to which 2 must be raised to get x.

It is the inverse of exp2(). Reach for it when the answer is naturally measured in bits or octaves — information content, the number of halvings in a binary search, the exponent of the nearest power of two.

Anchor values: log2(1) = 0, log2(2) = 1, log2(8) = 3, log2(0.5) = -1.

Domain:

  • x > 0 gives an ordinary result

  • x = 0 gives -inf

  • x < 0 gives NaN

An integer input is promoted to a floating-point result.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

Series or Series& The base-2 logarithm elementwise. log2_() overwrites the current storage.

Gradient¶

log2() is differentiable:

d/dx log2(x) = 1 / (x * ln 2)

That is the natural-log derivative 1/x scaled by 1 / ln 2 (about 1.4427). The gradient is large near x = 0 and shrinks as x grows.

In-Place Form¶

log2_() is the in-place sibling of log2(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — log2_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 8.0});

auto& ref = x.log2_();
std::cout << "x=" << x << "\n";
std::cout << std::boolalpha << "same object: " << (&ref == &x);

Output¶

x=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 1, 3]
same object: true

Examples¶

Example 1. Powers of two map to integers.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 8.0, 0.5}).log2());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 1.0000, 3.0000, -1.0000]

Example 2. The domain edges. 0 gives -inf, a negative gives NaN.

pluss::series::print(std::cout, pluss::make_series({0.0, -1.0}).log2());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-inf, nan]

Example 3. The backward multiplier is 1 / (x * ln 2).

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 4.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

x.log2().sum().reverse();

std::cout << "dx=" << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1.442695, 0.72134752, 0.36067376]

Each entry is 1.442695 / x, since 1 / ln 2 = 1.442695.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • log2(0) is -inf and log2(x < 0) is NaN; neither throws.

  • The result is floating point even for an integer input.

  • For a natural-log quantity use log(); for base 10 use log10(). They differ only by a constant scale.

Summary¶

log2(x) is the base-2 logarithm:

  • inverse of exp2()

  • -inf at 0, NaN for negatives

  • promotes integer input to floating point

  • differentiable, backward multiplier 1 / (x * ln 2)

See Also¶

  • Series::exp2: the inverse.

  • Series::log: natural logarithm; base-2 is this scaled by 1 / ln 2.

  • Series::log10: base-10 logarithm.
